newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Japan sees little chance for WTO labour agreement.
newsitem.headline: Japan sees little chance for WTO labour agreement.

text.p: The effort to link trade and international labour standards faces an uphill battle at the World Trade Organisation (WTO) Ministerial Conference, a Japanese Foreign Ministry official said on Monday.
The United States is pushing hard to use international trade rules to raise Third World labour standards, eradicate sweat shops and stop an estimated 250 million children working.
But many developing countries say the issue is a protectionist ploy and argue both their economies and their workers would be worse off with such rules.

The Japanese official told reporters just a mere mention of the issue in the final declaration was meeting stiff resistance. "There are a number of countries which are still opposing even a reference," he said.
He said Japan would be willing to accept a mention, but "there is such a strong objection" that he thought personally it might not happen.
The WTO was not necessarily the best forum to pursue the issue, and the International Labour Organisation might be more appropriate, the Japanese official said.

Labour standards are just one of the issues being discussed this week by trade ministers from the 128 members of the WTO. Among others are liberalisation of government procurement policy and removing tariffs on information technology.

Japan agrees with the United States in wanting an Information Technology Agreement (ITA) that would scrap tariffs on an estimated $1 trillion worth of annual world trade in computer and telecommunications products.

The official criticised the European Union (EU) for seeking concessions in such areas as liberalisation of government procurement policies in exchange for agreeing to ITA reductions in tariffs on semiconducters.
"That position we cannot accept," he said.
He added, however, that Japan would like to see agreement on more transparency in government procurement so it is clear to all what policies individual countries are pursuing.
He expressed hope the meeting would also agree to establish a working group to look at investment and competition policy, issues Japan has been pushing.

Japan's Trade Minister Shinji Sato is absent from the WTO deliberations due to a domestic scandal, but Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda is scheduled to speak on Tuesday and expected to have several bilateral meetings with key players.
